passage: Pallavi, you asked why grown-ups fight. Let me tell you about me as a girl of nine. Every night my parents' voices rose behind their door, and I was sure it was my doing, because of my poor maths marks and the socks I left on the floor. I began folding my clothes each night and studying until my eyes burned, trying to be better. One evening I finally asked Amma, "Are you fighting because of me?" She hugged me hard. "Never. That is between your father and me, and nothing you do could cause it." I cried, but my shoulders felt lighter. Children think everything is theirs to fix, Pallavi. If you wonder, ask. -- Himani

qa.q: What did Himani begin doing each night at the age of nine?
qa.a: She began folding her clothes each night and studying until her eyes burned.

qa.q: How did Himani feel about her parents' fights as a girl?
qa.a: Himani felt guilty and worried, sure the fights were her fault because of her maths marks and socks, so she tried hard to be better until she asked Amma.

qa.q: What should a parent say when a child wonders if the fighting is their fault?
qa.a: A parent should say clearly that it is between the adults and nothing the child does could cause it, as Amma told Himani.

qa.q: How might Pallavi feel on hearing this story?
qa.a: Pallavi may feel reassured that another child once had the same worry, and that it is alright to ask; Himani ends by telling Pallavi to ask if there is a wondering.

grounding: An elder recalls blaming herself for her parents' fighting until her mother told her plainly it was not her doing.

passage:
"Papa, can I ask something?"
Hemant looked up from the dishes. "Of course, Thomas."
"When you and Mummy shouted last night... was it because of my report card?"
Hemant turned off the tap. "Why do you think that?"
"Because you said 'his marks' and then it got louder."
Hemant dried his hands and sat down next to him. "Listen carefully. Mummy and I were arguing about grown-up things. Money, work, how tired we are. Your marks came up for one second. But our fights are not because of you. Not your marks, not your room, nothing you did."
Thomas's shoulders dropped. "Promise?"
"Promise. It's our job to sort it out, not yours."

qa.q: What did Thomas hear Papa say that made him worried?
qa.a: He heard Papa say "his marks" before it got louder.
He was afraid and guilty, thinking the fight was his fault because of his report card.

qa.q: What did Hemant do that helped Thomas?
qa.a: He stopped what he was doing, sat down, and told Thomas clearly that the fights were not his fault and that it was the parents' job to sort it out.

qa.q: How might Hemant have felt when Thomas asked his question?
qa.a: Hemant may have felt sad and a bit guilty that Thomas had been carrying that worry.

grounding: A boy wonders if his parents' fighting is because of his marks; when he asks, his father tells him clearly that it is not his fault.

passage:
My name is Ramesh, and when I was nine, my parents argued almost every night. I was sure it was because of me. Maybe because I left my toys all over the floor, or because I forgot my homework so often.
So I became perfect. I made my bed without being asked. I kept my room spotless. My younger brother Omkar thought I'd gone strange.
But they still argued.
One night, Omkar asked Ma straight out: "Are you fighting because of us?" She knelt down and said, "No. Never. You two have nothing to do with it. These are grown-up problems."
I felt something heavy slip off my back. I let myself leave one sock on the floor.

qa.q: Why did Ramesh try to be perfect?
qa.a: Ramesh felt guilty and anxious, believing the arguments were caused by the mess and forgotten homework.

qa.q: What made the biggest difference to Ramesh?
qa.a: Ma saying clearly that the children had nothing to do with it and that these were grown-up problems.

qa.q: How might Omkar have seen his sibling's sudden perfect behaviour?
qa.a: Omkar thought Ramesh had gone strange, not understanding the worry behind it.

grounding: A child blames themselves for the parents' fighting and tries to be perfect, until a parent says clearly it is not the children's fault.
